members.name: cdk_lower_node
members.doc:
Lowering one node by dispatching on its kind: the AST the calc parser

binaries kind 20, and the op name in `.name` picks the opcode. The

members.name: cdk_lower
members.doc:
The full lower: text to IR, or the Err naming the refusing parse
stage. The IrFunction handed back is caller-owned (free_ir_function).

members.name: cdk_emit_text
members.doc:
The emitted text: one line per instruction, `dest = name args`, with
ir_opcode_name for the mnemonic. The text leaves the Buffer: the
caller owns it and frees it with free_str.

SPELLING CONSTRAINED BY THE STAGE: this takes the IrFunction by value
because a read of an array field through a struct POINTER parameter
(`f.blocks[0]` where `f: &IrFunction`) segfaults both stage compilers
while the reference lowers it -- the scalar `f.next_temp` read and the
`f.blocks[0] = blk` store through the pointer both lower fine, which
is how cdk_lower_node stays a pointer. The by-value copy shares the
array header word, so nothing is duplicated.

members.name: cdk_eval_ir
members.doc:
The interpreter: each instruction reads its sources from the slot
table and writes its dest, exactly like the register walk the emitted
text names. The answers come from the IR, never from the AST. It
takes the function by value for the same stage-side Array field reads
via pointer parameters that cdk_emit_text documents; the copy shares
the blocks header.

members.name: calc_compile

caller's free_str has something it owns.

members.name: calc_eval

The run shape the issue names: source, evaluated. A malformed input

members.signature: pub fun write_string(path: string, content: string) <bool>
members.doc:
`fputs` and not `fwrite`: a `string` is NUL-terminated and carries no length,
so `write_string` writes up to an embedded NUL and cannot preserve bytes past
it. For binary content use `stdio::std`'s `File::write_text(path, text,
count)`, which takes the count explicitly, or `copy_file` for a whole file.
Adding a length here would change the signature, which 1.0.x does not do.

members.name: mkdir_p
members.doc:
`mkdir -p`: every missing directory on the way to `path` is created, each
prefix spelled with `substr` (fresh, freed here). A prefix that already
exists is not a failure, because that is what `-p` means; the empty root of
an absolute path is skipped the same way.

members.name: rename_path

members.name: mk_tmp_dir
members.doc:
A fresh uniquely-named directory under the platform's temporary directory.
On POSIX, `mk_tmp_dir("finfs")` spellings
build `/tmp/finfs` followed by the six characters `mkdtemp` overwrites, so
no call ever touches a fixed path and the caller's cwd stays clean. The
template must live in writable memory, so it is spelled through a `[char]`
buffer (`to_chars`) and the answer is cloned out of that buffer before it
is released -- the pointer `mkdtemp` returns points inside it. A null
prefix or an already taken template answers null, the routine miss.

members.name: walk_dir
members.doc:
The entries of one directory (not recursive), with `.` and `..` left out,
in the directory's order. POSIX record offsets follow the selected target
ABI, never inode or filename bytes. Windows reads WIN32_FIND_DATAA's name
at byte 44 in its 320-byte record. Both passes close their directory handles.

members.doc: The two constants that are otherwise a `cast<double>` at every use.

members.name: gcd
members.signature: pub fun gcd(a: int, b: int) <int>
members.doc:
Euclid, iteratively, in `long`. Absolute values first because `%` on a negative left
operand is negative here: without it `gcd(-12, 18)` would be -6.

The widening is what makes the magnitude representable. `gcd(-2147483648, 0)` is 2^31,
which is one past the largest `int`, and negating `-2147483648` in an `int` wraps back
to itself -- so the absolute-value step has to happen where the value fits. The result
is refused rather than returned wrapped, the way `isqrt` refuses a negative radicand:
a negative "greatest common divisor" is a wrong answer, not a boundary.

members.name: lcm
members.signature: pub fun lcm(a: int, b: int) <int>
members.doc:
`gcd` is what makes this safe from overflow for the inputs it can represent: dividing
before multiplying keeps the intermediate no larger than the result. The sign is folded
in `long` for the same reason `gcd` needs it: negating `-2147483648` in an `int` is a
wrap, so the magnitude is computed where it fits and then checked.

members.name: ipow
members.signature: pub fun ipow(base: int, exponent: int) <int>
members.doc:
Integer exponentiation. Does not check for overflow -- nothing in the language traps it
and there is no wider type to promote to -- but a negative exponent has no integer
answer at all, so that is refused.

members.name: isqrt
members.doc:
The largest `n` with `n * n <= value`. A loop rather than Newton's method: the loop is
obviously right at the boundaries, which is where a clever version goes wrong.
`isqrt(15)` is 3 and `isqrt(16)` is 4.

The loop compares `guess + 1 <= value / (guess + 1)` instead of multiplying, which is
what keeps it in the documented domain. `(guess + 1) * (guess + 1)` overflows once the
guess reaches 46340 -- 46341 squared is 2147488281, past `INT_MAX` -- and a negative
product compares as "still <= value", so the loop never exits for a radicand near the
top of the range. The division form is the same test written where nothing overflows;
the cost is one integer division per step.

members.name: floor_div
members.signature: pub fun floor_div(a: int, b: int) <int>
members.doc:
Floor division and the remainder that goes with it, which is not what `/` and `%` give
for a negative operand: `-7 / 2` truncates toward zero and `-7 % 2` is negative. These
are the pair where the remainder always has the divisor's sign, which is what an index
wrapping into a table wants -- `hashmap.fin` folds a negative hash by hand for exactly
this reason.

The one input the hardware cannot divide is `-2147483648 / -1`: the quotient is 2^31,
one past the largest `int`, and x86 traps with SIGFPE before any comparison sees it.
The quotient refuses by name, the way `isqrt` refuses a negative radicand; the
remainder is exactly 0, because -1 divides the minimum evenly, so `floor_mod` answers
it instead of trapping.

members.name: Arena
members.doc:
---------------------------------------------------------------------------
Arena: one bump region, one free.

`create(bytes)` allocates the region ONCE; `arena_bytes(count)` bumps by
`count` bytes and hands the region's first cell back as `&char`. THE BUMP
NEVER REALLOCATES, so byte cells die together: `destroy()` is THE one free
of everything the bump served, with no per-object bookkeeping anywhere.
The `%c` a cell reads stays readable while the arena is non-destroyed, and
a cell used after `destroy()` is the caller's use-after-free -- the
ownership rule above, spelled nowhere better than here.

Alignment is EXPLICITLY not offered: an int needs a mod-4 offset, and the
bump's cursor advances by whatever `count` says; a caller who needs
alignment asks the module's... nothing, today (the typed routes with
fresh blocks are the only way an unaligned int stays impossible -- and
fresh blocks do not bump the byte cursor).

The MODULE-internal route the free functions take to the meter is
`admit(count)`; it exists so `arena_block`'s handout registers against the
byte cap in the unit the free function can express, which is COUNT QUANTUM
and not bytes -- see the `sizeof(T)` gap above: `count * sizeof(T)` would
be the honest multiply, and it lowers only on the reference backend.

members.name: Pool
members.doc:
---------------------------------------------------------------------------
Pool: fixed slots for hot types, a free list, no per-object allocs.

`create(capacity)` allocates ONE `[T]` array of slots and ONE `[int]`
array of free indices; `take()` pops an index, `give(index)` pushes it
back, and read/write touch the slot behind an index. The slots never
individually allocate or free, so a hot bucket's new/delete churn is
paid twice in the pool's life: two `new`s at create, one `delete` pair at
destroy. Same trick for the free list as for the cells: an array, not a
pointer chase, because `[int]` indexing is what lowers everywhere.

The issue's `Pool<T, N>` becomes `Pool::<T>(capacity)` here, and the gap
is the header's constant-spelling note. Exhaustion refuses with a blame
on `take` rather than answering with a pointer-that-does-not-exist,
because `[T]`-array indices have no null and a `&T` that answers nothing
is not a handout this interface can carry.

members.name: LibcAlloc
members.doc:
---------------------------------------------------------------------------
LibcAlloc: what `new`/`delete` already were, spelled as an allocator.

ADR 0003's "document current semantics" is exactly this: the default
allocator nobody wires is C's malloc through `new` and `free` through
`delete`, and the wrapper below does no more than count what it handed
out and spell the two directions. `malloc_bytes`/`grow_bytes`/`free_bytes`
are the raw chunks; `alloc`-as-in-compiler-blocks is `new [T, n]{}`
reached through the free functions of this module (`arena_block` has the
same body with a meter), and `used()` is the running total THIS wrapper
handed out -- libc's own bookkeeping stays libc's.

members.name: NullAlloc
members.doc:
---------------------------------------------------------------------------
NullAlloc: the allocator that always refuses.

The "what if allocation failed" harness's whole toolkit: every query
answers the impossible, and every handout aborts. The issue's recorded
intent -- measure the what-if path -- is this: the refusal happens HERE
with the allocator's name, so what a harness measures is that its
conditional-on-success logic took the branch that assumes failure, not
that malloc's NULL leaked through silently.

members.name: mem_malloc_bytes
members.doc:
The raw routes a caller reaches without the wrapper structs: same bodies,
same blames, no counting -- libc keeps its own books and the caller owns
the chunks.

modules.summary: Networking: TCP over IPv4, through POSIX sockets or Winsock 2.

members.name: Socket
members.doc:
`sockaddr_in` is its sixteen bytes in an `[int, 4]`. Word 0 is the C struct's
first two `short`s -- `sin_family` (host order) then `sin_port` (network
order) -- packed into one 32-bit store, and word 1 is `sin_addr`, stored
exactly as `inet_addr` answered it, which is already network order. Storing
the four bytes as bytes would have to know which end of an integer is which;
a store of the integer whose *bits* are those bytes does not, because the
platform writes it the same way C does. The port is packed through a `long`
so that the high byte's term does not overflow an `int` on the way in.

members.name: TcpStream
members.doc:
The connection a caller lives with, named the way the issue and every
tutorial name it. Thin by intent: every method forwards to `Socket`'s
plumbing so the wire ABI stays judged in exactly one place, and the
ruling stands (`blame` on failure, blocking, dotted-quad only).

members.name: TcpListener
members.doc:
The listening side, as thin as the stream side. An accepted listener begets
a `TcpStream`; the wrapper holds the listening descriptor the same way.

lit: consume the next token iff it carries `kind`, and answer whether

seq: consume `kinds` all in order or nothing at all -- a failed probe
rewinds through `position`/`seek` so the stream looks as if the
question was never asked.

members.name: join

members.name: basename
members.doc: libc owns basename/dirname with borrowed-result semantics; use namespaced symbols.

members.name: stem
members.doc:
The basename without its last extension: `stem("/a/b/foo.txt")` is `foo` and
`stem("/a/b/archive.tar.gz")` is `archive.tar`. A name with no extension --
including a dotfile like `.gitignore`, whose dot is at position 0 -- comes
back whole. Fresh memory; `free_path` releases it.

members.name: normalize
members.doc:
Collapses `.`, `..` and repeated separators without touching the filesystem:
`normalize("a//b/./c/../d")` is `a/b/d`, `normalize("/x/../../y")` is `/y`
(an absolute path clamps at its root), and a relative path that climbs past
its start keeps the excess -- `normalize("a/../..")` is `..`. An empty result
is `.` for a relative path and `/` for an absolute one, and a trailing
separator is dropped. Fresh memory; `free_path` releases it.

@ bundled Output, the `Printable` contract, the byte stream, and files.

members.name: print_str
members.doc:
The un-`Printable` forms, for the values that have no `format_str` and never will. A
caller printing a `string` or an `int` should not have to wrap it in a struct, and
`printf` with a hand-written format string is the alternative these replace -- the whole
point of the typed layer is that the format string is not the caller's problem.

members.name: print_bool
members.doc:
The `bool` the typed layer had no spelling for: `%d` renders it `1`/`0`, the
same convention `print_int` uses, so a caller printing a flag does not
hand-write a format string for it.

members.name: eprint_int
members.doc: The stderr half `print_int` never got. Same rendering, the other stream.

members.name: print_double
members.doc:
The floating-point half. `%g` gives the shortest round-tripping spelling --
`2.5` rather than `%f`'s `2.500000` -- the same choice `number2str_float` makes.

members.name: flush
members.doc:
`fflush(null)` flushes every open stream, which is what C specifies for a null argument.
It lowers, which is worth stating because a null passed to a pointer parameter is not
always accepted here.

members.name: read_line
members.doc:
One line from standard input, without its line ending. Null means end of
input with no bytes read, which is the only state a caller can tell apart
from an empty line: a blank line is `""`, a line whose last byte is `\n` or
`\r\n` loses that ending, and a final line without a newline is returned
whole. The buffer grows until the line ends, so no line is truncated at a
fixed size; a line that would pass the `int` limit refuses by name.

A `string` is NUL-terminated and carries no length, so a line containing a
NUL byte cannot be returned without silently cutting it at that point. That
is refused with "stdin line contains a NUL byte" rather than hidden -- the
same rule the backend invariant states for data that cannot be represented.
A caller reading binary input should use a byte-oriented reader.

The returned string is `calloc`ed and caller-owned; release it with
`strings::std`'s `free_str`, which is libc `free` under another name.

members.name: read_all
members.doc:
Everything left on standard input, byte for byte, in the same shape
`File::read_all` returns: a fresh `[char]` one longer than the content, with
the final byte a terminator, so `.length` is the byte count plus one. This is
the binary-safe stdin route -- `read_line` cannot return a NUL in a `string`,
and this one carries bytes in an array whose length is explicit. End of input
before any byte gives a one-element array, not null. Release with `delete`.

members.name: Stream
members.doc:
An in-memory byte stream. `stream_length` is how much content it holds and
`capacity()` is how large the buffer is; `expand` deliberately makes the second larger
than the first, which is why both exist.

members.name: File
members.doc:
Files, through C. Every method is `static` and takes a path, which is the shape the
draft writes; a `File` value that holds an open handle is a different design and this
module does not have the `&void`-field evidence to write it.

Measured end to end rather than type-checked: a scratch program writes five bytes,
reads `exists=1 size=5`, reads the bytes back through `read_all`, removes the file and
reads `exists=0`.

modules.summary: @ bundled Reference-counted strong handles and non-owning weak handles (ADR 0039). `release()` drops exactly one strong reference and frees the value at zero. Weak handles retain the shared counters, never the value; their `release()` frees the counters when neither strong nor weak references remain.

members.name: wptr
members.doc: The non-owning handle retains the counters until its explicit release.

members.name: len
members.doc:
The byte length, not counting the terminator. `s.length` does not lower, so this is
how a length is asked for.

members.name: equals
members.signature: pub fun equals(a: string, b: string) <bool>
members.doc: Content comparison, which is what `==` does not do. See the header.

members.name: compare
members.signature: pub fun compare(a: string, b: string) <int>
members.doc: Negative, zero or positive, as C's `strcmp` gives it -- the ordering a sort wants.

members.name: free_str
members.doc:
Frees a string this module returned. Named rather than left to the caller's own
`@define` of `free`, because every allocating function here says to call this one.

members.name: find
members.signature: pub fun find(haystack: string, needle: string) <int>
members.doc:
The byte offset of `needle`, or `-1`. Computed as a difference of lengths rather than of
pointers: pointer subtraction is not an operator this language has, and two `strlen`s
are.

members.name: contains
members.signature: pub fun contains(s: string, sub: string) <bool>

members.name: index_of_char
members.signature: pub fun index_of_char(s: string, c: char) <int>

members.name: last_index_of_char
members.signature: pub fun last_index_of_char(s: string, c: char) <int>

members.name: to_chars
members.doc:
A `string` as a NUL-terminated `[char]`, which is the only form whose bytes can be read
one at a time -- indexing a `&char` does not lower. The buffer is one longer than the
content, so `.length` is `len(s) + 1`. `delete` frees it.

members.name: from_chars
members.signature: pub fun from_chars(bytes: [char], start: int, count: int) <string>
members.doc:
A slice of a `[char]` as a fresh `string`. `&bytes[start]` is what makes a mid-buffer
slice expressible: a `[char]` does not cast to a `&char`, but the address of one of its
elements is a `&char`.

members.name: clone
members.doc: A fresh copy. The caller owns it; `free_str` releases it.

members.name: concat
members.signature: pub fun concat(a: string, b: string) <string>
members.doc:
`a` then `b`, in fresh memory. This is what `a + b` would be if `+` on a pointer
lowered.

members.name: substr
members.signature: pub fun substr(s: string, start: int, count: int) <string>
members.doc:
`count` bytes from `start`, clamped to what is there. A `start` past the end raises
rather than returning empty, because that is a caller's arithmetic error and an empty
string would hide it; a `count` past the end does not, because "to the end" is a
reasonable thing to ask for.

members.name: starts_with
members.signature: pub fun starts_with(s: string, prefix: string) <bool>

members.name: ends_with
members.signature: pub fun ends_with(s: string, suffix: string) <bool>

members.name: to_upper
members.doc:
Case conversion by comparison and offset, because `&` and `|` are not in the expression
grammar and the usual bit trick cannot be written. ASCII only, and that is a limit
rather than an oversight: a correct Unicode fold needs tables this library has no way to
carry.

members.name: replace_char
members.signature: pub fun replace_char(s: string, target: char, replacement: char) <string>
members.doc:
Every occurrence of one character replaced by another. Character-for-character rather
than substring-for-substring, because a substring replace changes the length and needs
a second pass to size the result; this is the half that is one pass.

members.name: repeat
members.signature: pub fun repeat(s: string, n: int) <string>

members.name: parse_float
members.doc:
A decimal `double` from `[+-]digits[.digits][eE[+-]digits]`, or an `Err`
naming why not. No allocation: the rejected case carries a literal, and the
accepted value is the `double` itself.

WHY THE GRAMMAR IS FIN'S AND NOT C'S. `strtod` accepts `inf`, `nan`, `0x10`,
leading whitespace, a trailing tail and a bare `.5`; every one of those is
either not a decimal number a Fin program should treat as a value or a
silently accepted half-parse. The walk below admits exactly the decimal
grammar and then hands the VETTED text to `strtod`, which is what makes the
conversion correctly rounded instead of a hand-rolled accumulation -- the
same shape json.fin's scanner uses, and the reason a wrong result here is
not possible for accepted text.

OVERFLOW AND UNDERFLOW ARE REFUSALS, NOT SATURATION. `strtod("1e999")` is
`+inf` with `ERANGE`; this module has no `errno`, so the test is the IEEE
one json.fin records (a finite value times zero is zero). An infinity is
"float overflow in parse_float". An exact zero from a mantissa with a
nonzero digit ("1e-999") cannot be told apart from a legitimate value by
magnitude alone, so the mantissa is checked: a nonzero significand that
converted to zero is "float underflow in parse_float". A genuine zero
("0", "-0.0", "0e10") has an all-zero significand and is accepted.

This is an `Outcome` and not a blame because the text is the caller's data;
`parse_int` blames for the same reason the module header gives it: no
`Outcome`-returning integer form exists yet, and changing it would break
1.0.x. The message on an Err is a string literal and must not be freed.

members.name: count
members.signature: pub fun count(s: string, sub: string) <int>

members.name: pad_left
members.signature: pub fun pad_left(s: string, width: int, pad_char: char) <string>

members.name: pad_right
members.signature: pub fun pad_right(s: string, width: int, pad_char: char) <string>

members.name: split
members.signature: pub fun split(s: string, separator: char) <&Collection<string>>
members.doc:
Splits on a single character. Always returns at least one part, and a separator at
either end produces an empty part there -- so `split("a,b,", ',')` is three parts, the
last empty, which is what makes `join(split(x, c), c)` give `x` back.

Every part is fresh memory and so is the `Collection`; a caller frees each part with
`free_str`.

members.name: join
members.doc:
The inverse of `split`, for any separator rather than a single character. Sizes the
result first and copies once, rather than concatenating in a loop -- which would
allocate and leak one intermediate per part.

members.name: split_str
members.signature: pub fun split_str(s: string, sep: string) <&Collection<string>>
members.doc:
Splits on a whole separator string rather than a single character. Matches
left to right without overlapping -- `split_str("aaa", "aa")` is `["", "a"]` --
and an empty separator returns the whole string as its one part, so
`join(split_str(x, s), s)` gives `x` back for any separator, the same round-trip
`split` documents for its character form.

Every part is fresh memory and so is the `Collection`; a caller frees each part
with `free_str` and the container with `delete`.

members.name: replace
members.signature: pub fun replace(s: string, needle: string, to: string) <string>
members.doc:
Replaces every non-overlapping occurrence of `needle` with `to`. An empty `needle`
matches everywhere, which no caller means, so it returns a fresh copy of `s`
instead of looping. The result is fresh memory; `free_str` releases it.

modules.summary: Sync: native threads, mutexes, and bounded channels.

members.name: Thread
members.doc:
One OS thread, identified by its native handle. Copies name the same thread,
so a `Thread` is handed to exactly one joiner,
the way a moved-from `File` is expected to stay closed.

members.name: Mutex
members.doc:
A mutex and the value it guards. The lock is a non-recursive native lock; the value is a plain field, so `lock` hands out its
address and the guard survives only as long as the unlocked caller
releases -- the compiler records no obligation.

v0 has no poisoning semantics: a panic under one lock's protection is
`blame`, which unwinds nothing, and the mutex outlives the aborted
process only because nothing outlives an aborted process.

members.name: Channel
members.doc:
A bounded channel: a locked ring of results. `send` refuses (false)
when the buffer is at capacity; `recv` waits for a value. Both take the
same mutex for a very short span, and the recv loop drops it around its
sleep so a sleeping waiter cannot hold the producer out.

The canonical single assertion: the name the guide writes when a test
has one thing to say. Same polarity as `blame` -- the argument is the
condition that must hold.

members.name: shrink
members.signature: pub fun shrink(prop: fn(int) -> bool, bad: int) <int>
members.doc:
The halving shrinker `for_all` reports through. Documented in this
file's header: the smallest failing input in the halving chain that
starts at `bad`, where a failing input is one the property does not
hold on. The walk assumes a nonnegative start; a negative `bad` has
no halving chain (negative halves round toward zero) and answers
unchanged.

members.name: for_all
members.signature: pub fun for_all(seed: int, n: int, gen: fn(int) -> int, prop: fn(int) -> bool) <noret>
members.doc:
The property runner. Inputs are `gen(seed + i)` for i in 0..n-1 -- a
negative `n` runs nothing -- and a passing property is silent. The
first failing input blames with the field solver's message:

  for_all: property failed at input F, minimally at M (halving shrink)

where M is `shrink(prop, F)`, so a run's stderr names both the first
failing input and the minimally failing one.

members.name: bench
members.signature: pub fun bench(name: string, iters: int, body: fn() -> noret) <noret>
members.doc:
The benchmark stub. Honest refusal: whole-second wall timing cannot
answer ns/op without lying about the magnitude, and #59 owns the
sub-second clock this needs. It refuses loudly instead of printing a
number the caller would repeat.

modules.summary: Time: system clock and execution delays.

members.name: diff_sec
members.signature: pub fun diff_sec(start: long, end: long) <long>

members.name: Duration
members.doc:
A fixed-width span of seconds. `nanos` is normalized to [0, 999999999] by
`Instant::elapsed`; a hand-built value outside that range still answers, it
just does not mean what the fields say.

members.name: Instant
members.doc:
A monotonic timestamp in nanoseconds. Copyable and comparable only with
itself: there is no wall-clock member, so it cannot be rendered, only
differenced.

members.name: format_rfc3339
members.doc:
Renders epoch seconds as `YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SSZ` (always UTC, no fractional
part, no offset). The date math is Howard Hinnant's days-from-civil inverse
in pure Fin, so no `gmtime` struct crosses the FFI. Returns fresh storage;
release it with `free_rfc3339`.

members.name: parse_rfc3339
members.doc:
Inverse of `format_rfc3339`: exactly `YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SSZ`, years 0000-9999.
Shape, digits, and calendar ranges are blamed; a leap second (`:60`) is
accepted. A `string` cannot be indexed, so the bytes are copied once through
`[char]`, the only indexable byte access; see strings.fin.

members.doc: Special tokens

members.name: TOKEN_CARET
members.doc:
Bitwise XOR: `^` (issue #67). Absent until the self-host scanner could emit
it, which is why `a ^ b` parsed on the C++ compiler and failed on stage1/2/3
-- a StageAgreement divergence rather than a diagnostics difference. 126 is
taken by nothing and 125 is TOKEN_ERROR, so the caret sits above the error
sentinel deliberately: kinds below TOKEN_ERROR are never renumbered, because
src/lexer/tokens.hpp and this table are read side by side and a shifted
number would silently repoint one operator at another's lowering.

members.name: TOKEN_ERROR
members.doc:
Scanner hard-error token: the lexer could not produce source for this span
(unterminated literal/comment, bad byte). The diagnostic text rides in
Token.text so the parser reports it instead of guessing.

members.name: SourceLocation

members.name: str2int
members.doc:
The other direction, which this module had no form of at all. Both follow C: a string
that parses to nothing gives 0, and there is no way to tell that from a string that
spells zero. That is C's ambiguity rather than this library's choice, and a caller who
needs to distinguish them checks the string first.
